Orthopedics · published research

Shoulder pain

Some adjunct trials report lower pain or better function, while a sham-controlled trial found no superiority for pain, range of motion, or function.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some adjunct trials report lower pain or better function, while a sham-controlled trial found no superiority for pain, range of motion, or function.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Pain > Shoulder category contains 49 unique titles: 36 human clinical publications, 10 reviews or meta-analyses, two protocols, and one letter. The clinical record mixes rotator-cuff and impingement symptoms, frozen shoulder, high-intensity laser, laser acupuncture, and conventional PBM. Reviews synthesize trials already counted in the category.

Human and clinical evidence

A 50-person randomized trial of 830-nm laser added to physiotherapy reported greater improvement in pain and function than physiotherapy alone, but no significant advantage in range of motion (Eslamian et al. 2012). A 52-person sham-controlled randomized trial found no superiority of laser treatment for pain, range of motion, or function (Dogan et al. 2010). A recent comprehensive review describes a heterogeneous shoulder literature, with results depending on diagnosis and modality rather than one consistent effect (Cidral-Filho et al. 2024). Exercise or physiotherapy co-interventions are common and matter when interpreting added effects.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the exact shoulder-pain category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The Eslamian trial used an 830-nm near-infrared laser at 4 J/cm² on up to ten painful points, with a total exposure of about five minutes, alongside physiotherapy. Other shoulder records use different wavelengths, schedules, and delivery approaches, including high-intensity laser and acupuncture-point application. These treatments should not be pooled as one PBM protocol.

Interpretation

Some trials show an added short-term pain or function effect, but sham-controlled results are mixed and evidence varies by shoulder diagnosis and modality.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term shoulder pain or function improvement with selected PBM adjuncts Very low for consistent effects across shoulder diagnoses and modalities
Publications and records49 unique titles in exact Pain > Shoulder category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 36 human publications, but it combines different shoulder diagnoses, protocols, comparators, and laser modalities. A small trial reported pain and function gains when PBM was added to physiotherapy, while a sham-controlled trial found no superiority. Diagnosis-specific trials with common outcomes and longer follow-up are needed.
